transcript_header:
Date: 2025-11-18
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Recording ID: ff-20251118-6b7c-ndf
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Thompson (Redwood AE), Ethan Cole (Redwood SE), Dr. Laila Yates (Northwest MedSys), Marcus Reed (NWMS IT Sec), Priya Singh (NWMS Compliance), Omar Velasquez (NWMS Infra)
summary: Discovery focused on feasibility of running Redwood Private in a disconnected, air-gapped environment within a regulated hospital network. Key concerns: offline update process (signed manifests), hardware constraints (NVMe capacity, GPU availability A100 vs H100), KMS/HSM integration, SOC2/ISO requirements, network egress policy, and validation/testing cadence. Redwood AE/SE outlined architecture options (private control plane with local agent, fully disconnected on-prem bundle) and next steps for docs and benchmarking.
topics: Air-gapped update mechanism and signed manifests
Hardware profile: GPUs, NVMe/SATA, RAM and NIC requirements
KMS/HSM and key management for offline environments
Validation: canary vs full rollout in disconnected site
Telemetry/observability when no egress is allowed
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, then we'll jump into the questions on the air-gapped setup.
[00:06] Laila (NWMS): Hi, I'm Laila, head of MLOps. Thanks.
[00:10] Marcus: Marcus here, IT security.
[00:13] Priya: Priya, compliance.
[00:15] Omar: Omar, infra.
[00:18] Ethan (Redwood SE): Hi all, Ethan from Redwood, I'll cover the technical bits.
[00:22] Maya: Great. To set the stage, can you describe current constraints — network egress, physical access, hardware inventory?
[00:30] Laila: Sure. We're a hospital system, many apps must be isolated. No outbound internet from the inference racks; updates have to be done via removable media or an approved jump box in a DMZ. Hardware is mixed — some racks have H100s, most have A100s; a couple of edge sites only have 1xA100 or none and use CPU fallback. Storage is NVMe for the model nodes but limited to 8 TB per node.
[01:02] Maya: Understood. When you say "no outbound internet", do you allow signed manifests to be staged via an approved USB or via an operator workstation in the DMZ?
[01:11] Priya: We prefer staged media. Compliance wants an auditable chain — manifests signed by our key, and we keep a copy in our audit repository. HSM integration is preferred.
[01:21] Ethan: That lines up with a disconnected workflow we've done before. Two options: (1) a fully offline package you push to nodes with a local agent that validates a signed manifest and applies the update, or (2) a private control plane that runs in your VPC but talks to Redwood over a constrained channel — though looks like you want the fully offline route.
[01:40] Marcus: Yes, fully offline. We can't have even telemetry that leaves the site without approval. But we still want logs and metrics locally and a way to pull them out for audits.
[01:49] Maya: Ok. For fully offline, we support a bundle that includes: model weights, runtime, container images, and a signed manifest. The manifest includes hashes and a signature chain. The local agent verifies before applying and writes an audit record plus local sig verification.
[02:05] Laila: How do you handle model deltas? We want small updates rather than shipping 100s of GB repeatedly.
[02:12] Ethan: We can produce delta updates for certain quantized formats — e.g., patching tokenizer or small layers. Full model swaps still necessary for architectural changes. For very constrained NVMe, we recommend staging on external NVMe media or using model sharding across nodes. There's tradeoffs with KV cache warmup.
[02:31] Omar: About hardware: our older racks have PCIe v3 NVMe and one dual-slot GPU. Cold start memory for large models is concerning. Can Redwood run with CPU-only fallback in a degraded mode?
[02:42] Ethan: Yes, we have a CPU fallback, but throughput and latency will degrade significantly. For critical latency-sensitive paths we recommend at least 1 GPU per serving cluster. Another strategy is to use smaller quantized models for edge racks.
[02:55] Marcus: Security wise, our SOC2 requires KMS keys to never leave HSM. How do you integrate with an HSM in an air-gapped context?
[03:03] Maya: Good question. For private/on-prem we can support customer-managed keys stored in an HSM. The signing process can happen offline — you sign the manifest with a key stored in the HSM, and the local agent verifies the signature using a public key bundle. We also support an option where the HSM provides attestations.
[03:19] Priya: Do you support PKCS#11?
[03:22] Ethan: Yes, PKCS#11 support is available for the integration points we use in the packaging flow. There's a small shim for the offline signer.
[03:28] Laila: What's the recommended GPU and disk profile for our primary cluster? We run 2k reqs/day, but spikes matter — ER triage workflows are latency-sensitive at 100-200 qps bursts.
[03:39] Ethan: For bursty loads I'd recommend a 4xA100 or 2xH100 rack for the main serving pool. NVMe at least 10 TB aggregate to host multiple models and checkpoints. For cost balance, mix Dedicated-like reserved capacity on the racks with smaller edge nodes with A100s. H100 gives better throughput per card, but compatibility and availability are factors.
[04:00] Omar: Our procurement says H100 lead time is months. So A100 will be default. Does Redwood have quantized kernels tuned for A100?
[04:08] Ethan: Yes, we've tuned quantized kernels for both A100 and H100 families. Performance delta varies by model and sequence length — we'll send a benchmark matrix.
[04:15] Maya: We'll include a benchmarking checklist — sequence lengths, batch sizes, cold/warm KV cache expectations. We'll also recommend batch/latency SLOs per model.
[04:23] Marcus: About observability offline — we still need structured logs, token-level cost data, and per-route latency histograms but stored locally. Is there a console we can host internally?
[04:32] Maya: Yes, the Redwood Private bundle includes an optional internal console you can run behind your firewall. It aggregates local metrics and exposes dashboards. For strictly offline sites, you host it in your DMZ or management VLAN. Exporting audit logs is a manual pull or via an approved extractor.
[04:48] Priya: Who has access to the console? We need RBAC and SSO tied to Okta.
[04:52] Ethan: RBAC is supported and we support SAML/OIDC against Okta. For fully offline, you can integrate against an internal IdP or manage users locally.
[05:02] Laila: For updates, can we run a staged canary rollout across 3 racks and then promote?
[05:06] Ethan: Yes, even offline you can do staged rollouts. The manifest can contain rollout flags and the local agent supports canary policies. Promotion happens once you validate local metrics.
[05:16] Marcus: How do we validate model drift/regression without telemetry out? We want to run evaluation harnesses internally.
[05:23] Maya: We recommend shipping a validation bundle with an eval dataset and scripts that run locally post-deploy; the agent will run the tests and place results in the audit folder. You can then extract them for the compliance team.
[05:33] Omar: One concern: firmware updates for NIC or GPUs sometimes block our maintenance windows. Does Redwood's offline bundle require specific driver versions?
[05:41] Ethan: The runtime has minimum driver/CUDA requirements, and we'll include a hardware compatibility matrix. For the most part, we've been able to support a range of driver versions but major runtime optimizations may need newer drivers. We'll highlight those in the compatibility doc.
[05:55] Laila: Regarding model caching: if we have limited NVMe, can Redwood use a network-mounted cache on a separate storage node inside the isolated network?
[06:03] Ethan: Yes, you can configure shared NVMe or an NFS head for model artifacts. We recommend high-throughput network fabric (RDMA) for KV cache. But if that's not available, local NVMe per node is more predictable.
[06:16] Maya: Quick callout — some transcription artifacts: KV cache sometimes shows up as "KV cash" in our transcriptions, ignore that haha.
[06:22] (laughter)
[06:25] Priya: Are there legal/signature requirements we should be aware of for the signed manifests?
[06:29] Maya: The manifest is a cryptographic artifact. We can provide a signing template and a recommended attestation policy. For legal, many customers treat manifest signing as part of their change control; Redwood's template includes a signature timestamp and operator ID.
[06:42] Marcus: What about emergency rollback? If an update causes regressions and we have no egress, how fast can we revert?
[06:49] Ethan: The local agent keeps a previous-image cache and can rollback to the prior runtime/model state. Rollback times depend on model size and IO; typical rollback under 15 minutes for up to 50 GB on NVMe, but can be longer for larger images. We'll provide exact numbers for your model sizes.
[07:06] Laila: Can we do A/B testing in this environment?
[07:09] Ethan: Yes, routing policies can be local. The local control plane supports A/B and percentage-based splits, just config driven.
[07:17] Priya: For audit logs, is the format JSONL? We need to retain immutable logs for 7 years per regulation.
[07:23] Maya: Logs are JSONL and we can configure retention and export scripts. For immutable retention, we'd recommend writing to WORM-certified media in your archive process.
[07:34] Omar: On the topic of maintenance: can we schedule offline package builds or do you only provide one-off images?
[07:40] Maya: We can automate package creation — Redwood Ops can push a release bundle on a cadence or per-commit. For Air-gapped, you typically approve bundles and then we generate signed manifests which you retrieve through an operator flow.
[07:53] Laila: How much work is the initial install? We have limited SRE bandwidth.
[07:58] Ethan: Initial install usually takes a couple of days for the first rack with our SE assistance, less for subsequent racks. We provide step-by-step runbooks and can do remote sessions. For air-gapped installs we do a combination of on-site and pre-packaged instructions.
[08:10] Marcus: Regarding data residency: model prompts and responses must not leave the site. How do you enforce that?
[08:15] Maya: In Private deployments, you host the entire inference stack; nothing leaves unless you explicitly export. The default agent disables outbound endpoints. If you run internal console in DMZ, you can control export policies.
[08:27] Laila: Any known limitations we should flag to procurement/execs?
[08:31] Ethan: Main ones: initial integration effort, hardware procurement lead times (especially for H100), and operational changes for offline validations. Cost profile is different compared to hosted; there's more fixed cost in hardware and ops. We'll provide a TCO sketch.
[08:46] Maya: We'll include a one-pager on differences hosted vs dedicated vs private offline.
[08:49] Priya: For compliance artifacts, can you provide SOC2 attestation, ISO docs, and sample audit reports?
[08:55] Maya: Yes, we'll share SOC2 and ISO artifacts, and a sanitized audit log example. For private/on-prem you rely on your own compliance posture, but Redwood provides supporting docs.
[09:06] Laila: One last technical: does the runtime support model quantization formats like int8 and PTQ?
[09:12] Ethan: Yes, INT8 and Q4_0 type quantizations are supported; performance varies by model. We'll include guidance for which quant profile to use given your memory constraints.
[09:22] Omar: We have a question about operator authentication for applying updates. Can only certain operators run the apply step?
[09:28] Ethan: The manifest and the agent enforce operator identity. You can require two-person approval by signing manifests with two keys or by requiring an Okta workflow prior to staging.
[09:39] Maya: Great. Time check — we have about 10 minutes left; any remaining blockers?
[09:44] Priya: Just want to confirm the audit chain — manifest signature, agent verification, test run, and immutable log.
[09:51] Maya: Yes. We'll provide a sequence diagram.
[09:54] Marcus: We'll also need the benchmarking checklist and the compatibility matrix.
[09:59] Maya: Noted. Ethan, anything to add?
[10:01] Ethan: I'll add a note about KV cache warmup times and suggested preloading strategies. Also will document recommended batch sizes for burst QPS.
[10:10] Laila: Sounds good. We'll return the rack inventory and maintenance windows.
[10:13] Maya: Perfect. Let's recap next steps...
[10:18] (brief recap follows)
[10:20] Maya: Recap: Maya sends flow diagrams and compliance artifacts; Ethan sends benchmark checklist and driver/compatibility matrix; Omar sends hardware inventory; schedule follow-up security deep dive.
[10:31] Priya: Thanks all.
[10:33] Laila: Thanks, bye.
[10:35] End of recording.

Notes on transcript: occasional mis-heard words (e.g., "KV cash" instead of "KV cache"), speaker overlap at 06:22; some technical acronyms expanded later in follow-ups.
